newsitem.title: KENYA: ZAIRE FOREIGN FORCE - redundant before it lands?
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE FOREIGN FORCE - redundant before it lands?

text.p: Simple arithmetic dictates that the mass migration of Hutu refugees back to Rwanda has lessened and perhaps ended the need for a costly multinational force with a confused mission.
By the time the first foreign troops may be ready to deploy next week, more than half the 1.1 million Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire are likely to have returned home voluntarily.
The United States contingent is almost certain to have nothing to do in the northern Goma sector where it reluctantly accepted minimalist and almost risk-free duties.

The trickier and more dangerous job in the southern Bukavu and Uvira sectors still exists. As many as 500,000 refugees there probably need urgent help but the key volunteer, France, is not wanted by Rwanda or the rebels in control on the ground.
Canada, designated as leader of the military task force with a humanitarian mandate, will have to decide if last week's plans still make sense.
Even if common sense suggests they do not, is the lumbering military mission stoppable?
On Sunday an advance party of 34 Canadian soldiers arrived in Kigali, capital of Zaire's eastern neighbour and foe Rwanda, to set up a headquarters for the force.
"The situation is very fluid, the movement of the refugees has had a big impact on what is happening, but we have just to carry on with our plan which is to 'recce' out sites," Major Rod Babuik said.
Rwanda, so far the big winners from a month of dramatic changes in eastern Zaire, no longer wants the force.

"Our position is that the force was coming to create this corridor for the refugees to come home and now they are coming home. So we don't see any need for the force to come," said presidential spokesman Joseph Bideri.
Washington and South Africa, both sceptics from the outset, must be hoping the Hutus put a spring in their step as they trudge back to the homeland they left in panic in 1994.
"If this trend continues, it will change substantially the nature of the humanitarian problem" in Zaire, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Sunday.

The force of up to 10,000 soldiers was authorised by the U.N. Security Council on Friday to bring aid to refugees stranded in eastern Zaire. Yet hours before the vote the problem was already diminishing with the Hutu reverse exodus.

Initially 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus and 100,000 Burundian Hutus were trapped in Zaire's North and South Kivu provinces by a month-long rebellion. By Sunday morning the total was down by at least 20 percent as Rwandan Hutus in North Kivu's Goma area crossed the border and returned home in relief or trepidation.
A similar crowd was peacefully following in their footsteps. Some aid agencies believe almost all the 730,000 Rwandans living in North Kivu before the rebellion will cross.

Ironically the mass movement was caused by the force's ultra-safe mandate. Troops would not disarm the Hutu gunmen among the refugees or separate them from ordinary folk who might want to go home, the U.S. and Canada said.

The rebels heard this last Wednesday night and knew it meant the Hutus would be able to stay in Zaire indefinitely once the foreign force arrived. So on Thursday morning they bombarded the main refugee camp at Mugunga and the next day the Hutus started streaming home.

"It was clear to Rwanda and their rebel allies in east Zaire they had to race against the clock to destroy Mugunga before the force arrived," a Kenya-based refugee spokesman, Chris Nzabandora, told Reuters.

The U.N. special envoy on the Zaire crisis, Canadian Raymond Chretien, argued on Sunday a force was still needed. But South Africa's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki, disclosed in Rome that countries due to send troops would review the mission.
Mbeki said the review would not take place until Wednesday. For a force whose genesis was marked by foot-dragging, this adds another three days for the voluntary repatriation to continue.

The force's advocates can still point to the uncertainty about the fate of the half-million Hutus further south. But they could be scattered over a huge area -- nobody knows where they are and what their intentions are.
Rebels control the area and have made crystal-clear that French troops -- the leading volunteers -- should not come.

"France has political ends to feed. They want to maintain a regime we are trying to defeat. We are not opposed to the ideal of humanitarian existence but we must beware of colonial crocodile tears," rebel leader Laurent Kabila said last week.
